{"id": "2:200/q19", "question": "How does the worldly-prayer clause connect to the command?", "turns_on": "Whether it divides present pilgrims or compares different historical believers.", "positions": [{"id": "2:200/q19/p1", "position": "It divides the addressed pilgrims or supplicants by what they seek.", "reasons": "The fa marks a division for Ibn Ashur; Abu Hayyan says supplication, unlike praise, admits a worldly-only and a two-world form, and rejects a Sufi third group that makes no request. Ibn Kathir says prayer follows remembrance at a responsive time. The groups include Muslims and polytheists before 9:28. Abu Hayyan says the shift from direct address to third person excludes people whose worldly-only prayer is unworthy of a rational addressee."}, {"id": "2:200/q19/p2", "position": "It contrasts those remembering God before the Prophet's mission with believers after it.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports this historical reading but prefers a division among pilgrims."}]}
{"id": "2:200/q20", "question": "How is min al-nās man yaqūlu parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether man is subject, adjective or agent.", "positions": [{"id": "2:200/q20/p1", "position": "Man is the subject, with the preceding prepositional phrase as predicate; yaqūlu is its relative clause.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Qurtubi permit subject status; Samin calls it strongest."}, {"id": "2:200/q20/p2", "position": "Man is an adjectival or indefinite noun qualified by the following clause.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Qurtubi and Samin record this analysis."}, {"id": "2:200/q20/p3", "position": "Man can function as an agent.", "reasons": "Samin attributes the option to al-Akhfash."}]}
{"id": "2:200/q21", "question": "Why does the supplication use plural 'us' with singular man?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:200/q21/p1", "position": "Man is singular in form but plural in meaning, so a group says 'grant us'.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says singular prayer might suggest few worldly seekers; Samin says the clause follows meaning rather than form. Biqai says the later singular pronoun follows form and suggests few of this community will be lost."}]}
{"id": "2:200/q22", "question": "Who are the people who ask only for this world?", "turns_on": "Whether the historical referent is polytheists specifically or the warning also includes believers.", "positions": [{"id": "2:200/q22/p1", "position": "Historically they are polytheists or disbelieving pre-Islamic pilgrims.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Wahidi and Ibn Ashur say disbelief in resurrection explains their sole worldly concern; Ibn Zayd distinguishes the Messenger, unbelievers and hypocrites. Ibn Abbas describes Bedouin requests at the pilgrimage standing."}, {"id": "2:200/q22/p2", "position": "The warning can also apply to a believer who confines supplication and effort to worldly aims.", "reasons": "Qurtubi says such a believer lacks a share like the one who seeks the afterlife; Qatada describes a servant working for this world; Tabatabai speaks of generic people, including unbelievers."}]}
{"id": "2:200/q23", "question": "What do the worldly-only petitioners ask for?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:200/q23/p1", "position": "Worldly goods such as provision, wealth, livestock, servants, status, rain, victory, safe travel and offspring.", "reasons": "Mujahid names victory and provision; Anas reports naked circumambulators asking for rain, victory and safe return; Ibn Abbas lists fertile years and children. {"id": "2:200/q24", "question": "How is the object of ātinā understood?", "turns_on": "Whether a second object is omitted or fī is altered.", "positions": [{"id": "2:200/q24/p1", "position": "The second object is omitted: grant us whatever worldly benefit we seek.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Tha'labi, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Biqai say the request is left general or understood. Kuran Yolu explains the omission as indiscriminate desire; Zajjaj pauses at ātinā because it is supplication."}, {"id": "2:200/q24/p2", "position": "Fī means min, making the request 'give us from the world'.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Samin reject this alternative because it improperly omits both objects."}, {"id": "2:200/q24/p3", "position": "Fī is extra, making the world the direct object.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Samin reject the parse; Abu Hayyan says only one object can be suppressed."}, {"id": "2:200/q24/p4", "position": "An implied continuation says God grants what He chooses rather than necessarily the request.", "reasons": "Biqai records this alternative to a simple unstated object."}]}
{"id": "2:200/q25", "question": "Is 'says' literal speech or an inward disposition?", "turns_on": "Whether the prayer is spoken or represents a person's state.", "positions": [{"id": "2:200/q25/p1", "position": "It depicts a person's inward aim, whether or not the words are spoken.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the worldly seeker treats desire as good, while the seeker of God asks only for genuine good."}, {"id": "2:200/q25/p2", "position": "It recounts actual prayers made at Hajj.", "reasons": "Anas, Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr relate spoken requests for rain, offspring, camels and sheep."}]}
{"id": "2:200/q26", "question": "What does 'no share in the Hereafter' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether it denies a reward there or describes a refusal to seek one.", "positions": [{"id": "2:200/q26/p1", "position": "They receive no share of good, divine reward or Paradise there.", "reasons": "Tabari says they traded the afterlife for worldly adornment; Baydawi says their concern is confined here; Tabatabai infers their works are nullified, contrasting 2:201–202 and citing 25:23, 46:20 and 18:105. Ibn Kathir says the warning deters imitation."}, {"id": "2:200/q26/p2", "position": "They have no desire to seek an afterlife share.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan records this as an alternative sense; Biqai says they neither desire nor strive for it, and Elmalılı says they ask for none."}]}
{"id": "2:200/q27", "question": "What does khalāq mean?", "turns_on": "Whether it denotes an allotted share, an abundant share, or a share sought or merited.", "positions": [{"id": "2:200/q27/p1", "position": "An allotted share or portion of good.", "reasons": "Muqatil cites 9:69; Tabrisi derives a measured entitlement and also relates it to khuluq, noble character; Ibn Abbas cites a line by Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt and parallel verses. Harali relates the share to created nature and character."}, {"id": "2:200/q27/p2", "position": "A substantial or abundant share of good.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Tabrisi specify abundance, explaining the force of denying khalāq."}, {"id": "2:200/q27/p3", "position": "A sought share or allotment.", "reasons": "Baydawi records this alternate nuance."}]}
{"id": "2:200/q28", "question": "What is the syntax of min khalāq and fī l-ākhirah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:200/q28/p1", "position": "Min before khalāq is extra after negation, making the denial comprehensive.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi and Qurtubi describe the construction."}, {"id": "2:200/q28/p2", "position": "Khalāq is the subject, lahu its predicate, and fī l-ākhirah attaches to the predicate or is circumstantial.", "reasons": "Tabrisi gives both attachments."}]}
{"id": "2:200/q29", "question": "What follows for prayer and life from the contrast with 2:201?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:200/q29/p1", "position": "Seek good in both lives, not solely this world's benefits.", "reasons": "Tabari says ask God's pleasure in both; Wahidi, Durr and Ibn Zayd contrast the two prayers. {"id": "2:200/q31", "question": "How does this passage connect with neighboring verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:200/q31/p1", "position": "The remembrance and supplicant contrast continues into 2:201–204 and later seekers of God's pleasure.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd identifies a third group in 2:204; Abu Hayyan says 2:204–207 contrasts sweet speech with a person who gives himself for God, so outward speech should match belief; Tabatabai says God swiftly grants according to the servant's aim. {"id": "2:219/q01", "question": "Who asked about wine and gambling, and why?", "turns_on": "Reports differ in the named questioners and their stated motive.", "positions": [{"id": "2:219/q01/p1", "position": "Companions, often named as ʿUmar and Muʿādh, asked because wine impairs reason and gambling consumes wealth.", "reasons": "MUQATIL (author): The verse was revealed concerning Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ali ibn Abi Talib, and several Helpers; maysir means gambling. THALABI (عمر بن الخطاب ومعاذ بن جبل): Umar, Muadh, and several Ansar asked the Prophet for a ruling on wine and gambling, saying they destroy reason and consume wealth; the verse was revealed in response. MAWARDI-FULL (author): Māwardī says the Companions asked Muhammad about wine and gambling, and that this was the first verse revealed on the subject. WAHIDI-ASBAB (author): Al-Wahidi reports that Umar, Muadh ibn Jabal, and some Ansar asked Muhammad for guidance about wine and gambling, saying both impair reason and consume wealth. WAHIDI-BASIT (عمر بن الخطاب ومعاذ بن جبل وسعد بن أبي وقاص): The verse was revealed after Umar, Muʿadh, Saʿd, and others asked the Prophet about wine and gambling, saying they impair reason and take wealth. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (عمر، ومعاذ، وسعد بن أبي وقاص): ʿUmar, Muʿādh, and Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ asked the Messenger for a ruling because wine and gambling destroy reason and strip away wealth. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): The verse was revealed after ʿUmar, Muʿādh ibn Jabal, and a group of Anṣār asked about wine and gambling because they impair reason and consume wealth. KASHSHAF-FULL (عمر ومعاذ ونفر من الصحابة): Umar, Muadh, and other Companions asked for a ruling because wine destroys reason and property; the verse about sin and benefit followed, and some drank while others abstained. TABRISI (جماعة من الصحابة): A group of Companions asked the Prophet about wine and gambling because they destroy reason and strip away wealth; this verse was revealed in response. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (عمر بن الخطاب): One occasion report says ʿUmar asked God to give a decisive clarification about wine, after which this verse was revealed. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الأنصار وعمر ومعاذ): Another occasion report says a group of Anṣār, including ʿUmar and Muʿādh, asked the Prophet for a ruling because wine removes reason and takes away wealth; this verse was revealed. RAZI-FULL (عمر ومعاذ ونفر من الصحابة): A report of the staged prohibition says wine was initially lawful, then Umar, Muadh, and other Companions asked for a ruling because it ruins reason and wealth, prompting this verse; some drank and others abstained. | mentions 16:67 RAZI-FULL (author): Because Umar and Muadh sought a ruling on wine as a destroyer of reason and wealth, Razi argues that anything with the same effect must be wine or share its ruling. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): A chronology says the earlier verse about date and grape products led Muslims to drink; Umar, Muadh, and other Companions asked about wine, and this verse followed. | mentions 1, 6, :, 6, 7 NASAFI-FULL (author): The author recounts the stages: the first Meccan verse (16:67) allowed intoxicants; after Umar and others asked about wine’s harm, this verse followed. Some drank and others abstained. | mentions 16:67 ABUHAYYAN-FULL (عمر ومعاذ): The occasion reported is that ʿUmar and Muʿādh asked the Prophet for a ruling on wine and gambling, saying they destroy reason and strip away wealth. DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says the Companions asked only thirteen questions before the Prophet's death, all answered in the Quran, including wine and gambling, sacred months, orphans, menstruation, spoils, and spending; they asked about what benefited them. | mentions 2:217, 2:220, 2:222, 8:1 SUYUTI-LUBAB (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās reports that companions ordered to spend in God's cause asked what portion of their wealth they should give; the answer was to spend the surplus. BURSEVI (المفسرون): After ʿUmar, Muʿādh, and other Companions asked about wine because it removes reason, the verse on wine and gambling was revealed; some tried to take its benefits while avoiding its sin, while others abstained. BURSEVI (عمر بن الخطاب): ʿUmar donated half his wealth to outdo Abū Bakr, but when asked what remained for his family he said half; Abū Bakr gave everything, saying Allah and His Messenger remained for them, and ʿUmar conceded he would not compete again. ALUSI-FULL (الواحدى): Al-Wāḥidī says ʿUmar, Muʿādh ibn Jabal, and a group of Anṣār asked the Prophet for a ruling because wine and gambling destroy reason and consume wealth; this verse was revealed. ELMALILI (Hazret-i Ömer ve Muâz ve diğer bazı ashâb-ı kirâm): Umar, Muadh, and other Companions sought a ruling because wine removes reason, occasioning this verse. ELMALILI (author): ʿUmar, Muʿādh, and other Companions asked the Prophet for a ruling on wine because it removes the intellect; this verse was revealed. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (Hz. Ömer ve birçok sahâbî): Umar and many Companions repeatedly asked for clarification about wine and gambling; their requests are cited among the occasions for the successive explanatory and prohibitory revelations. | mentions 5:90"}, {"id": "2:219/q01/p2", "position": "Other reports name a different set or portray a general request for clarification.", "reasons": "MUJAHID (مجاهد): Mujahid calls this the first occasion on which wine was censured. THALABI (عائشة): Jisra bint Dajaja reports Aisha repeatedly saying she does not permit an intoxicant, even if made from bread, when asked about alternating batches of nabidh. THALABI (ابن عباس): Asked about bazidh, Ibn Abbas says whatever intoxicates is forbidden. WAHIDI-BASIT (مقاتل): A further derivation takes maysir from ease because people shared a camel to make its cost easier; Muqatil says they asked to split its price. BAGHAWI-FULL (ابن عباس): When asked about bādhīq, Ibn ʿAbbās says Muhammad had already ruled on it: anything intoxicating is forbidden. RAZI-FULL (عبد الرحمن بن عوف): At a meal hosted by Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, guests drank, became intoxicated, and one recited the opening of al-Kafirun incorrectly; this occasioned the prayer-time restriction. | mentions 4:43 QURTUBI-FULL (author): The questioners about wine and gambling are believers, as Qurtubi noted earlier. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The plural verb is used although the reported questioners were two, since Arabic can attribute one person’s act to a group. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The believers asked the Messenger about wine and gambling as God had foretold; the answer that both involve grave sin was meant to lead them to abstain and indicates their prohibition. BIQAI-FULL (author): The author says wine was among the spoils taken by Abdullah ibn Jahsh's expedition, which occasioned the preceding verses. BIQAI-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): When a woman asked what she could give from her husband's wealth, the Prophet answered fresh fruit: it may be eaten or gifted before it spoils. SUYUTI-LUBAB (يحيى): Yaḥyā relates that Muʿādh b. Jabal and Thaʿlaba asked what to spend f

{"id": "2:219/q02", "question": "Why does the answer use قُلْ?", "turns_on": "The formula may be explained as a response pattern or as an honor to Muhammad.", "positions": [{"id": "2:219/q02/p1", "position": "The explicit command honors Muhammad as the addressee and confirms his prophetic delivery of revelation.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL (author): The explicit command qul functions as a seal confirming Muhammad's prophethood and honoring him as God's addressee for delivering revelation. | mentions 2:217, 2:219, 2:220, 2:222, 8:1, 18:83, 10:53, 4:176"}, {"id": "2:219/q02/p2", "position": "The verse belongs to a pattern of question-answer formulas using qul, fa-qul, or no stated formula.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL (author): Razi distinguishes four answer forms: replies introduced by qul, by fa-qul, questions with no stated answer, and answers without either formula; he illustrates them with the cited questions. | mentions 2:217, 2:219, 2:220, 2:222, 8:1, 18:83, 10:53, 4:176, 2:186, 7:187, 20:105"}]}
{"id": "2:219/q03", "question": "What exactly was being asked about wine and gambling?", "turns_on": "Whether the question seeks a ruling, a definition, or the consequences of the practices.", "positions": [{"id": "2:219/q03/p1", "position": "The question sought their ruling or permissibility, including the acts of drinking and gambling.", "reasons": "BAGHAWI-FULL (author): The verse was revealed after ʿUmar, Muʿādh ibn Jabal, and a group of Anṣār asked about wine and gambling because they impair reason and consume wealth. RAZI-FULL (author): Razi answers that the question concerns wine generally, so its sin necessarily accompanies it under every circumstance; drinking entails that forbidden consequence and is itself forbidden. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): A chronology says the earlier verse about date and grape products led Muslims to drink; Umar, Muadh, and other Companions asked about wine, and this verse followed. | mentions 1, 6, :, 6, 7 BAYDAWI-FULL (author): The question is about engaging in wine and gambling, as shown by the answer’s reference to what is in both. NASAFI-FULL (author): The author recounts the stages: the first Meccan verse (16:67) allowed intoxicants; after Umar and others asked about wine’s harm, this verse followed. Some drank and others abstained. | mentions 16:67 ABUHAYYAN-FULL (بعض من ألف في الناسخ والمنسوخ): Some works on abrogation say most scholars regard this verse as abrogating the prior permissibility of wine, setting aside the Meccan Anʿām passage. | mentions 6:145 ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): As with wine and gambling, some benefit from a forbidden thing does not establish permissibility. SAMIN-DURR (author): A noun is omitted after عن: the question concerns the ruling on wine and gambling, including permissibility or prohibition, not the substances themselves; the answer matches that understood question. DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says the Companions asked only thirteen questions before the Prophet's death, all answered in the Quran, including wine and gambling, sacred months, orphans, menstruation, spoils, and spending; they asked about what benefited them. | mentions 2:217, 2:220, 2:222, 8:1 BURSEVI (author): The question is about the ruling on consuming wine, since permissibility, prohibition, sin, and obedience attach to accountable acts, not to objects in themselves; the ruling also covers sale and purchase. BURSEVI (المفسرون): After ʿUmar, Muʿādh, and other Companions asked about wine because it removes reason, the verse on wine and gambling was revealed; some tried to take its benefits while avoiding its sin, while others abstained. ALUSI-FULL (author): The question concerns engaging in wine and gambling, as the answer’s “in them” makes clear; their sin comes from leading to neglected duties and committed prohibitions."}, {"id": "2:219/q03/p2", "position": "The question asked what these practices are or what follows from them.", "reasons": "KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The question concerns the consequences of engaging in wine and gambling, as indicated by the following explanation of their sin and benefit. RAZI-FULL (author): The question does not specify whether it asks what wine and gambling are, whether they may be used, or whether drinking is lawful; the answer about sin implies a question about permissibility. NASAFI-FULL (author): The question concerns the consequences of participating in drinking and gambling, as shown by the answer about sin and benefits. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): They ask about the legal status, permissibility, and use of wine and gambling, not about what substances they are; the answer therefore addresses their ruling."}]}
{"id": "2:219/q04", "question": "What does ٱلْخَمْرِ mean and how is its name explained?", "turns_on": "Whether khamr is a broad Arabic name for intoxication or a narrower beverage name; the root is explained through covering, mixing, or maturation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:219/q04/p1", "position": "Khamr is every intoxicant or drink that clouds the intellect; its name relates to covering the mind.", "reasons": "TAB-FULL (ابن زيد): Ibn Zayd says the passage was superseded by three verses in al-Māʾida and discusses the Prophet’s wine punishment: he treated it as a hadd by his judgment, not a fixed, named hadd. | mentions 5:90 ZAJJAJ (author): Wine is the agreed case; by analogy, anything that acts like it is also called khamr and has the same prohibition. ZAJJAJ (author): Khamr is named from covering: it applies to what veils a person, a woman’s veil, a prayer mat covering the face, and dough covered by fermentation. ZAJJAJ (author): Wine is prohibited by the Qur’anic text because it is called a great sin, and God explicitly forbids sin; Zajjāj cites 7:33 despite consensus. | mentions 7:33 IBNABIHATIM (عمر بن الخطاب): Umar says wine's prohibition concerned products of grapes, honey, dates, wheat, and barley, and defines wine as whatever overwhelms the intellect. IBNABIHATIM (أنس بن مالك): Anas reports that people drank wine after the initial verse, then left it when the prohibition in al-Ma'ida was announced; their drink was date nabidh called fadikh. | mentions 5:90 FARISI-HUJJA (author): Wine is not linguistically identical to nabīdh; primary names are not assigned by analogy, as Abū al-Aswad’s poem calls wine its sister. THALABI (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): They support this with Abu Hurayra's report that the Prophet said wine comes from the date palm and grapevine. THALABI (أبو عبد الرحمن): Abu Abd al-Rahman says the well-known Abd al-Malik report conflicts with al-Zubayr's version: Ibn Umar reports the Prophet saying every intoxicant is forbidden and every intoxicant is wine. THALABI (مالك والشافعي وأحمد بن حنبل وأبو ثور وأكثر أهل الآثار): They define wine as every intoxicating drink, whether grape-based or otherwise, and forbid any amount; its drinker receives the penalty except for the specified cooked drink after a third evaporates, whose testimony remains valid.
